paras.text: Claims Clocks and DIFS, Audio Lecture

Welcome to the claims clocks chapter. This turns Michigan insurance law into a calendar you can use on a real file. If you remember nothing else, remember this: almost none of Michigan's claims clocks start by themselves. They start when a specific piece of paper reaches the insurance company. A notice of loss. A proof of loss. A written demand. Wait for the carrier's own estimate before sending anything and you have handed it the calendar. That idea is the spine of this chapter.

Start at the beginning. A loss happens. Under M C L five hundred point two eight three three, subsection one, letter l, every Michigan fire policy must contain, quote, the notification requirements when a loss occurs, end quote. Notice what that does not say: how many days the insured has to report. The day count lives in the policy's conditions section. So if someone asks how many days a homeowner has under Michigan statute, the honest answer is that the statute sets no number. Read the policy.

Now here is where it gets interesting, because once that notice of loss lands on the insurer's desk, the insurer has its own clock running. M C L five hundred point two zero zero six, subsection three, says the insurer shall specify in writing the materials that constitute a satisfactory proof of loss not later than thirty days after receipt of a claim, unless the claim is settled within those thirty days. Thirty days, from receipt of the claim itself, meaning the notice, not from receipt of a proof of loss. So the moment a homeowner reports a loss, a thirty day clock starts on the insurer to tell her in writing exactly what documents it needs. Be careful here, because there is a shortcut people repeat that is wrong. You will hear that if the insurer stays silent past day thirty, whatever proof of loss the homeowner later submits automatically counts as satisfactory, and that Griswold says so. Griswold says the opposite: whether a satisfactory proof of loss was received is a question of fact. The thirty day duty is still worth a lot. It is a dated obligation the carrier either met or did not, and it locks in the document list the carrier said it needed. That subsection has a second rule too: if a proof of loss covers only part of the claim, that part is timely paid if paid within sixty days of receipt, and any later piece gets its own fresh sixty day clock. This is why smart strategy splits a claim into the undisputed part and the fought over part.

A separate clock sits in the mortgagee clause. Under M C L five hundred point two eight three three, subsection one, letter j, if a loss is payable to a named mortgagee and the insured fails to render a proof of loss, the insurer can notify the mortgagee, which then has sixty days after that notice to render its own. It only matters if the insured never submits her own. If she does, the mortgagee clock never turns on. And do not confuse it with an insured's own proof of loss deadline; the statute sets none. Sixty days belongs to the mortgagee alone, as a backstop.

Now money, because the two most confused clocks in the chapter live here. Two numbers, thirty and sixty, measuring different things. The thirty day clock, in M C L five hundred point two eight three three, subsection one, letter p, and echoed in M C L five hundred point two eight three six, subsection two, says the loss is payable within thirty days after receipt of proof of the amount of loss. That is the payment deadline.

The sixty day clock is different. It comes from M C L five hundred point two zero zero six, subsection four, and it governs when twelve percent simple interest starts piling up on unpaid benefits, from a date sixty days after satisfactory proof of loss was received, if the claimant is the insured or a person directly entitled to benefits. So here's the trap. A claim paid on day forty five is late under the thirty day payment rule but may owe zero interest, because interest doesn't start until day sixty one. Lateness and interest are not the same thing. Another critical detail: the reasonably in dispute defense, which normally lets an insurer off the hook for an unfair trade practice, does not apply to this twelve percent when the claimant is a first party insured. It is written only into the sentence about third party tort claimants. Two cases nail this down: Griswold Properties versus Lexington Insurance Company, two seventy six Michigan Appeals five fifty one, and Nickola versus M I C General Insurance Company, five hundred Michigan one fifteen, at the Supreme Court. Both hold a first party insured gets the twelve percent regardless of dispute. And no published Michigan property case extends that right to a restoration contractor holding an assignment of benefits. It belongs to the insured.

Now appraisal, the mechanism Michigan uses to resolve a pure dollar dispute without court. M C L five hundred point two eight three three, subsection one, letter m, has two key day counts, twenty and fifteen. After a written demand, each side has twenty days to name a competent, independent appraiser and tell the other side who it picked. Those two then try to agree on a neutral umpire. If they cannot within fifteen days, either party can ask a circuit judge, in the county where the loss occurred or the property sits, to pick one. Whatever any two of those three sign off on in writing becomes the amount of the loss. Each side pays its own appraiser; the umpire's cost and other appraisal expenses split fifty fifty. Remember what appraisal decides: only the amount, never whether the loss is covered. That distinction comes from Auto Owners Insurance Company versus Kwaiser, one hundred ninety Michigan Appeals four hundred eighty two, where the court said flatly that the issue of coverage is for the court, not the appraisers.

Now cancellation, where two statutes overlap and students get confused about which controls. M C L five hundred point two eight three three, subsection one, letter i, is the fire policy's own built-in cancellation clause. The insurer can cancel at any time by mailing notice not less than ten days before cancellation, postage prepaid, tendering or promising to refund the excess earned premium. Ten days is the floor every fire policy must contain as a contract term, that is, what the policy must say. For an actual homeowner's policy that is not the end of it. The Essential Insurance Act, chapter twenty one, layers an effectiveness rule on top for what it calls home insurance. M C L five hundred point two one two three says a termination isn't effective unless the insurer mails written notice at least thirty days before the termination date, except a notice given inside the policy's first fifty five days can be effective in as little as twenty days, and nonpayment notices follow whatever the policy itself says. And termination is a defined word, at M C L five hundred point two one zero four, subsection five: a refusal to continue to insure for reasons other than nonpayment of premium. That is why nonpayment sits outside the thirty day rule. DIFS spells this out in bulletin twenty twenty five dash twelve dash I N S, on insurers using aerial imagery to assess roof condition, saying that canceling or nonrenewing home insurance for reasons other than nonpayment triggers the thirty day rule, and the reasons must come from the closed list in M C L five hundred point two one one seven: not being an eligible person, physical condition and occupancy, a changed adjacent hazard, claim history, and underinsurance. That list does not include cosmetic roof discoloration seen in a satellite photo. The bulletin says almost exactly that: mere cosmetic roof issues, like discoloration or streaking, are not valid grounds for cancellation or nonrenewal. And on the claim history ground, here is a number that will catch you if you read only the statute. The statute still prints three thousand and four thousand dollars as the three year paid claim minimums. Those are stale. Subsection five tells the director to raise them with inflation every sixth year and certify the new figures in a bulletin, and bulletin twenty twenty four dash zero two dash I N S did that. Since January first, twenty twenty four, the real numbers are five thousand dollars excluding weather related claims and six thousand six hundred including them, with the next adjustment due in twenty thirty. Classic superseded figure trap: the statute is real, the number inside it is not.

Now the one year suit clock, which has a twist that trips people up. M C L five hundred point two eight three three, subsection one, letter q, says an action under the policy must be commenced within one year after the loss, or within whatever longer period the policy itself specifies. But that one year period is tolled, meaning the clock pauses, from the moment the insured notifies the insurer of the loss until the insurer formally denies liability. Picture a loss January fifth, notice January sixth. If the insurer never formally denies, only that single day counts against the year, and the clock stays frozen the whole time the claim sits open. If a clear formal denial arrives six months later, the remaining days run again from that date. A partial payment with a reservation of rights is not, by itself, a formal denial. A letter saying the company considers the file closed reads much closer to one. The statute never defines formally denies, so calendar every ambiguous letter as if it might be the one that restarts the clock.

Now the regulator itself, the Department of Insurance and Financial Services, or DIFS. Its complaint page describes the Office of Consumer Services as providing consumer information, investigating complaints, and assisting consumers in resolving them whenever possible, after first encouraging people to try the carrier directly. You can file online or by mail, email, or fax; the call center runs Monday through Friday, eight to five. But here is the honest limit you need to know cold. What DIFS says it does is investigate and help resolve. What its own bulletin twenty twenty five dash twenty five dash I N S says it can bring down on a carrier is fines, and suspension or revocation of the carrier's certificate of authority. Notice what is missing. Nothing DIFS publishes says it can decide whether your loss is covered, order a specific payment, or act as your attorney. Do not promise a homeowner any of the three. Nowhere on that page does DIFS promise a number of days for its own response either, or for forcing a carrier to answer, so if someone tells you DIFS makes carriers answer within thirty days, that is not supported by anything DIFS publishes. And the statute behind the enforcement, section twenty twenty six, reaches conduct other than isolated incidents showing a persistent tendency, so one badly handled file is not by itself the violation.

One more line worth memorizing. Young versus Michigan Mutual Insurance Company holds an insured has no independent cause of action under section twenty twenty six, the fourteen unfair practices, because that section exists to give the regulator authority over continuing practices. But the same case approves a private suit to recover the interest penalty under section twenty zero six. The twelve percent you can sue for. The fourteen practices you cannot.

A quieter statute works in the background too: M C L five hundred point two zero two six, subsection two. It is an unfair practice for an insurer to fail to keep a complete record of every insured complaint since its last examination, with the total count, classification by line, the nature of each, its disposition, and the time it took to process. So a certified letter of complaint straight to the carrier, even before or instead of DIFS, creates a paper trail the company must log.

Two topics outside the Insurance Code show up constantly in real Michigan claims. First, if a homeowner's mortgage is owned by Fannie Mae, the check usually goes to the servicer first, because of the mortgagee clause. Fannie Mae's Servicing Guide, section B dash five dash zero one, Insured Loss Events, tells servicers how to release it. If the loan is current or less than thirty one days behind, the servicer can release an initial payment up to the greater of forty thousand dollars, thirty three percent of total proceeds, or whatever exceeds the loan's remaining balance plus interest and advances, then the rest in draws tied to repair inspections. If the loan is thirty one days or more behind, small proceeds of five thousand dollars or less can go out in one payment, but anything larger gets an initial release of only twenty five percent of the proceeds, capped at the greater of ten thousand dollars or the amount above the loan payoff, with the rest released in twenty five percent increments after inspections and a required final inspection. Critically, servicers must prohibit paying a public adjuster or other third party fee out of proceeds unless Fannie Mae approves it in writing first. That is a private investor rule, not Michigan law. It binds the servicer, not the insurer, and it is often why a homeowner wins the statutory thirty day payment fight and still waits weeks for cash.

Second, understand what a DIFS bulletin is legally. Not a statute. It is the director's interpretive guidance on how DIFS reads and enforces the Insurance Code, replaceable by the next bulletin with no legislative vote. That cuts both ways: a bulletin can also be the only place a statutory number's live version lives, as with the five thousand and six thousand six hundred figures. Bulletin twenty twenty four dash twenty six dash I N S says that starting with homeowners and dwelling policies issued or renewed on or after July first, twenty twenty five, an insurer depreciating what it calls nontangible items, meaning labor, taxes, fees, and overhead and profit, in actual cash value must do it through a separate, optional, lower premium endorsement naming those items, rather than burying it in policy definitions. That conditions the practice; it does not ban it. Bulletin twenty twenty five dash twenty five dash I N S says dragging out claims administration or making unreasonable proof of loss demands to gain leverage violates the Code, citing section twenty twenty six, but it is written around auto claims, not property. And bulletin twenty twenty six dash sixteen dash I N S sets the fire insurance maximum escrow under M C L five hundred point two two two seven at twenty five thousand ninety dollars for July first, twenty twenty six through June thirtieth, twenty twenty seven. Do not confuse it with the separate calendar year escrow under M C L five hundred point two eight four five, which bulletin twenty twenty five dash twenty seven dash I N S sets at sixteen thousand three hundred eighty three dollars for twenty twenty six. Two provisions, two amounts, two periods.

To recap. Notice starts the insurer's thirty day duty to specify proof of loss requirements, and starts tolling the one year suit clock. Proof of the amount of loss starts two clocks: thirty days to pay, sixty days before twelve percent interest begins. An amount dispute can go to appraisal, twenty days to name an appraiser, fifteen more to agree on an umpire. Fire policy cancellation needs at least ten days notice, but a home insurance cancellation or nonrenewal for reasons other than nonpayment needs at least thirty, tied to the closed list in section twenty one one seven, whose claim history dollars are five thousand and six thousand six hundred, not the three thousand and four thousand printed in the statute. And the suit clock sits frozen from notice until a formal denial arrives. Master that sequence and you have mastered this chapter.
